name: Kaupaloki
powers: Brings success and fair fortune in buying and selling.
description: Kaupaloki, the 'trade-luck stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn for success in buying and selling. Merchants and farmers drew or carved the stave so that bargains would turn in their favour, a piece of practical magic in a seafaring and trading society where a fair deal was a matter of survival. It belongs to the group of luck-giving galdrastafir, distinct from the protective and aggressive staves of the same grimoires, and it was carried on paper, wood, or metal when goods went to market. Like most of the staves, its earliest known source is a 19th-century collection of older material, and it is now reproduced in books and on jewellery as an emblem of Icelandic folk magic. The Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík keeps the trade staves among its displays of the everyday uses of magic.
source: Huld manuscript (Lbs 4626 8vo, 1860)

name: Hymir's Cauldron
powers: Deep enough to brew ale for all the gods at a single feast.
description: The great cauldron of the giant Hymir, fetched by Thor and Týr so that the gods could brew ale enough for a feast. Hymiskviða says it was a mile deep; when Hymir refused to give it up, Thor took the kettle and carried it away. The same visit produced the god's famous fishing for the Midgard serpent Jörmungandr. The poem is one of the most comic of the Eddic tales: Thor eats a pair of oxen at the giant's table, breaks Hymir's cups by shattering them against a stone pillar, and finally lifts the great kettle from its post and walks off with it. In Snorri's retelling the story explains why Thor is expected to supply a cauldron for the gods' feasts, and the mile-deep kettle became a byword for the impossible scale of the giants' household goods.
source: Poetic Edda (Hymiskviða)

name: Knotted Rope Charm
maker: Tied by a 'wise' seller or Sami sorcerer
powers: Untying a knot raises wind; the third knot calls a storm.
description: A rope or cord with three knots, tied by a 'wise' seller and sold to sailors as a wind charm. Untying the first knot raised a gentle wind, the second a stronger breeze, and the third a storm, so prudent captains kept the third knot tied. The three-knotted wind cord is documented in Nordic and Sami maritime folklore and was often credited to Lapp (Sami) sorcery. Olaus Magnus drew and described the custom in 1555: a seaman from the north sold a cord of three knots to sea captains, warning that the third must never be loosed unless the ship stood in danger. The poet Petter Dass and later collectors repeated the account, and the 'wind knot' appears in accounts of Finnish and Sami magic, where the seller was sometimes said to have learned the skill from the Sami themselves. Frazer gathered the custom as the classic example of sympathetic wind magic, in which loosening a knot looses the wind the knot had bound.
source: Nordic maritime folklore on wind magic

name: The Kettle of the Underjordiska
powers: Returned filled with gold, or borrowed at a price.
description: A pot or kettle that the underjordiska, the hidden people beneath the earth, were said to borrow from farm households. In Swedish legend a woman lends a kettle to the hidden folk, often for a christening or a feast in their underground halls, and finds it returned filled with gold, a silver gift, or the sweet smell of their food — or learns that borrowing from them carries its own price. The motif of the borrowed vessel, known across Scandinavia, plays on the housewife's neighbourly duty to the hidden people and her reward or punishment for how she meets it. If she gave generously and asked no questions she was blessed; if she grudged the loan or told the world about it, the kettle came back fouled or the farm's luck turned. The borrowed kettle is one of the commonest objects in the story-world of the underjordiska.
source: Swedish legends of the underjordiska

name: Kubbestol
description: A Norwegian chair hollowed from a single upright log, with seat, back, and arms carved from the same piece of wood, often decorated with chip-carving and floral patterns. Kubbestol chairs stood in farmhouses as the seat of honor and were even used as the bridal chair at weddings. They show the woodcarver's art also seen in stave church portals and seter crafts. The chair is made from the trunk of a thick pine or birch, the heart cut out to form the seat while the bark and the shape of the log keep the outer form, and the arms grow out of the same block so that the whole chair is one piece of wood. The carving, with its roses, leaves, and interlaced bands, made each chair a signed work of its maker, and a well-carved kubbestol was handed down in the family for generations. It is the most famous piece of Norwegian folk furniture and a showpiece of the old carving tradition.
source: Norwegian folk furniture; museum collections

name: Karagoz
material: Dyed translucent leather (camel hide) on a stick
powers: Comic everyman of the shadow screen, bickering with Hacivat in plays performed behind a lit panel.
description: Karagöz, the shadow puppet of Ottoman Turkish theatre, gives its name to the traditional play performed behind a lit cotton screen with flat, articulated figures of dyed translucent camel hide worked on sticks, which cast coloured shadows as the single puppeteer, the hayali, moves them. The hero Karagöz, a bald, rough-spoken everyman, bickers endlessly with his polite, wordy friend Hacivat, and their exchanges of puns and misunderstandings drive the comedy, framed by music, song, and a stock cast drawn from the Ottoman city. Popular legend, recorded from the 17th century onward, is sometimes said to trace the form to two workers, an ironworker called Karagöz and a bricklayer or timber seller called Hacivat, whose banter halted the building of a mosque, so that the sultan had them executed and a puppeteer conjured their shadows back onto a screen. The genre was performed in Ramadan and before the sultans. It remains a living oral-dramatic tradition of Turkey, inscribed on the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage.
source: Turkish oral tradition and documented Ottoman shadow theatre

name: The Knot of Isis
powers: Guards the wearer through the power of Isis.
description: The looped red tjet amulet, the 'girdle of Isis', worn by the living and the dead for the goddess's protection and said to be her blood, her girdle, or the knot of her dress. Spell 156 of the Book of the Dead directs that it be made of red jasper and placed on the neck of the deceased so that the might of Isis would guard the throat and chest. Red carnelian and faience tjets are common in New Kingdom burials, where they sit with the djed and ankh in protective groupings, and the sign itself often accompanies the goddess in temple reliefs. As the girdle that Isis is said to have used to protect the infant Horus in the marshes, the amulet carried the mother-goddess's care into every grave where it was laid.
source: Book of the Dead, spell 156; amulet deposits

name: The Khamsa
powers: Deflects the evil eye and brings blessing to its bearer.
description: The open-hand amulet of the Maghreb and the wider Middle East, called the Hand of Fatima after the Prophet's daughter in Muslim usage and the Hand of Miriam in Jewish usage, hung in homes, worn as jewelry, and painted on doorways, cradles, and vehicles against the evil eye. The silver khamsa was the standard talisman of North African Jews and Muslims alike, made in every register from plain sheet silver to fine filigree set with coral and enamel. The open palm, shared with the wider Mediterranean hand-amulet tradition, reaches back to Punic and ancient Near Eastern hands of blessing, so the form carries an ancient root beneath its later name. Today the khamsa has crossed into global fashion as a pendant and charm, while its protective use continues undiminished in the societies that gave it its name.
source: Maghrebi ethnographic collections

name: Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi
powers: Said to command the wind and fell whole fields of grass; one of the Three Sacred Treasures.
description: The legendary grass-cutting sword drawn from the tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi by the storm god Susanoo, who then offered it to his sister Amaterasu; it is the sword of the Three Sacred Treasures of the Japanese imperial regalia, with the mirror and the jewel. Its name, 'grass-cutter', recalls the later story of the hero Yamato Takeru, who escaped a burning field by using the blade to mow the grass and turn the fire back on his enemies. The sword is said to be kept at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya, where it is guarded and almost never shown, and no one outside the shrine has verified its state. Alongside the mirror and the jewel it stands for the martial virtue of the imperial line and for the divine descent of the throne, as told in the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki.
source: Kojiki; Nihon Shoki

name: Kitsune's Crescent Comb
powers: Reveals a fox in human form; granting it service or love
description: The crescent-shaped comb of Japanese legend is the small hair ornament that a shapeshifting kitsune is said to drop when its disguise is betrayed, and finding it is supposed to bring a strange fortune or a lasting bond with the fox. The comb appears again and again in tales of fox wives, in which a man marries a beautiful woman who turns out to be a fox in human form; at the crucial moment the tail is seen, or the comb is left behind when the wife vanishes, and the discovery ends the marriage. In some variants the man who keeps the comb may command the fox's service or its gratitude, while in others the comb proves the spirit nature of the householder and drives the fox away for good. Because the fox in Japanese belief is both a trickster and a messenger of the rice god Inari, the comb carries an ambiguous charge: it is a clue, a keepsake, and a token of a crossing between the animal and human worlds. The motif is old enough to appear in the earliest collections of Japanese fox tales, and it still shapes modern retellings in which a comb on a shrine step promises a fox encounter.
source: Kitsune folktale tradition (Genjimonogatari imagery)

name: Khaen
powers: Voice of lam song and festival celebration
description: The khaen is the free-reed mouth organ of Laos, built from rows of bamboo tubes bound around a wooden wind-chest, whose drone-and-melody sound is the soul of the Lao folk song called lam. The player breathes in and out through a single mouth-hole while covering the finger-holes of the tubes, producing the interlocking melody and drone that lam singers improvise against, and the instrument accompanies courtship, festivals, and ritual across Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao tradition says that the khaen shaped the speech and poetry of the people, and the instrument is central to the great courtship tradition of the khap and lam. In the origin legend the khaen was first made by a man who wanted to imitate the sound of the wind in the bamboo, and its seven-note scale is regarded as the seed of Lao musical thought. UNESCO has inscribed the khaen playing of the Lao people as intangible cultural heritage, and the instrument remains the emblem of Lao national music.
source: Lao musical tradition

name: K'awiil Scepter
powers: Invests the ruler with the lightning-god's authority.
description: The K'awiil scepter, often called the manikin scepter, is a short staff topped by a small figure of the Maya lightning god K'awiil, a deity shown with a mirror set in his forehead, an elongated snout and a serpent leg. Classic Maya rulers carried it as proof of divine kingship, and royal portraits at Copan, Tikal, Piedras Negras and Palenque show it held at accession and in dance rituals, its snake leg trailing to the ground. The forehead mirror links the scepter to the lightning that K'awiil sent forth, and the god himself belonged to the Palenque Triad of patron deities. Stelae record how the scepter was handed to a new king as part of the regalia that made him a living link between his people and the gods. Carved in stone or wood, its surviving depictions let scholars trace how the symbol of royal lightning passed across the Maya world over centuries.
source: Classic Maya stelae and painted ceramics

name: Kachina Doll
material: Carved cottonwood root with paint and feathers
powers: Brings the blessing of the katsinam spirits to children.
description: Kachina dolls, or katsina tihu in Hopi, are small figures carved from cottonwood root and painted with the attributes of the katsinam, the spirit beings who visit Hopi villages from the winter solstice until July. Given to children, especially girls, by katsina dancers, they are teaching objects rather than idols: each doll helps a child learn the identity, dress and power of a particular spirit. More than three hundred katsinam are known, from the gentle and humorous to the fierce ogre katsinam who discipline children. Since the late 1800s Hopi carvers have developed the craft into an internationally collected art, moving from small flat tihu to fully carved figures, yet the ceremonial gift remains the core of the tradition. To the Hopi the katsinam are ancestors and forces of the natural world, and the doll carries their blessing into the home.
source: Hopi oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Katsina Owl Doll
powers: Teaches children the ways of the night hunter spirit.
description: The owl katsina doll, or mongwau tihu in Hopi, is a carved and painted cottonwood figure of the owl spirit of the Hopi katsinam, given to children so they may learn the owl's identity and power. The owl is a night hunter whose eyes and voice mark it as a being of wisdom and, in some traditions, a messenger connected to the spirit world. Like all katsina tihu the doll is carved from the soft root of the cottonwood, a wood the Hopi link to water and moisture, and painted with the colours and markings of the particular spirit. The owl katsina appears among the hundreds of katsinam who visit the villages in season, and its doll carries the teaching of that visit into the home. Collectors prize such carvings, but to the Hopi the doll's first purpose remains the instruction of children in the ways of the spirits.
source: Hopi oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Kero
material: Carved wood, often with painted scenes
powers: Twin cups shared to seal alliance and honor the sun.
description: The kero is the paired ceremonial drinking cup of the Andes, a flared goblet most often carved from wood, drunk from in twos at rituals of alliance, hospitality and the great festivals of the Inca calendar. The paired cups were passed so that each party drank the other's offering, sealing friendship and reciprocal obligation, and the drink was usually chicha, the maize beer central to Andean ceremony. Inca nobles and officials received keros as marks of office, and the cups appear in colonial accounts as indispensable to the toasts that accompanied every treaty and celebration. After the Spanish conquest, colonial-era keros were painted with elaborate scenes of Inca life, rulers, animals and ceremony, creating a crucial record of how the empire remembered itself. The kero tradition survives among Andean communities, where the paired cup still seals the bonds of ayllu and fiesta.
source: Inca-period and colonial keros in museum collections

name: Kultrún
powers: Carries the heartbeat of the land into ceremony.
description: The kultrún is the sacred drum of the Mapuche of Chile and Argentina, a shallow wooden bowl covered with a hide head and beaten with a single stick or by hand, played almost exclusively by the machi, the ritual specialist and healer. Its head is painted with a quartered design, a cross and the four directions, which orients the ceremony and maps the structure of the Mapuche universe, and around it the ngillatun ceremony of prayer and thanks is built. The machi sounds the kultrún to summon the spirits, to guide healing rites called machitun, and to call the community into a single rhythm; the drum is so closely tied to the office that a machi's calling is said to announce itself partly through the drum. The instrument is treated with the respect owed a sacred object, carried into the center of the ceremonial circle and held close by its keeper. In the twenty-first century the kultrún remains central to Mapuche religious life and has also become a symbol of Indigenous identity and resistance in Chile.
source: Mapuche oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Kayak
material: Sealskin stretched over a wood or bone frame
powers: Carries its hunter silently across the open sea after seals.
description: The kayak is the one-man hunting boat of the Inuit, Yupik and Inupiat, a frame of wood or bone stretched tight with sealskin, so light and watertight that a single hunter could carry it, launch it alone, and paddle it silently across the open sea after seals, walrus and whales. The hunter sat in its small cockpit, wearing a skin parka lashed to the rim so that the boat sealed around him, and with his harpoon and lance he could hunt from the surface and even right the kayak in the Eskimo roll, turning it over and back with a twist of the paddle. The design was perfected over millennia and was one of the Arctic inventions that explorers and missionaries carried back to the world, giving the English word kayak from the Inuktitut qajaq. In legend the boat carries its own weight too: in the tale of Sedna, the sea mother, her father rows her out over the water in his kayak before she becomes the ruler of the sea beasts. The kayak remains a living Arctic boat, rebuilt in traditional materials for festivals and races.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic maritime records

name: Kente Cloth
description: Kente is the strip-woven cloth of the Asante and Ewe peoples of Ghana, built up from narrow bands of silk and cotton woven on narrow looms and sewn edge to edge into bold geometric patterns, each of which has a name and a proverb meaning. Weaving was traditionally a male craft tied to the royal court, and particular patterns were reserved for the king; the colors carry their own language, with gold for royalty, green for growth, red for passion or danger, and the cloth is worn for the great occasions of Akan life. The Asante origin tradition credits the spider Anansi with teaching the first weavers, and the name kente comes from the Akan word for the open basket that the patterns recall. Kwame Nkrumah wore kente at Ghana's independence, and the cloth has become a worldwide emblem of African identity, worn by leaders and diaspora communities alike. Every strip of kente is woven memory, pattern by pattern.
source: Asante oral tradition

name: Kuba Beaded Cup
material: Wood, glass beads, cowrie shells, brass studs
description: The beaded drinking cups of the Kuba kingdom of the Democratic Republic of the Congo are carved from wood and densely covered with cowrie shells, brass tacks, and patterns of imported glass beads in geometric bands. Owned by kings, titled nobles, and wealthy men, the cups were used in the court ceremonies where palm wine was shared, and they were kept among the treasured possessions of the palace or the lineage house. Some cups take the form of a human head or a pair of feet, while others are plain beakers, and the intricate beadwork set the craftsmen of the royal workshops apart from ordinary potters. In Kuba court culture, drinking vessels were markers of rank, and the most elaborate pieces announced the generosity and wealth of the man who poured from them. The cups entered museum collections during the colonial period, and beaded Kuba cups are now recognised as a high point of African decorative art.
source: Kuba court tradition; museum collections

name: Kuba Ndop Royal Figure
description: The ndop is a carved wooden portrait figure of a Kuba king of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, showing the ruler seated cross-legged on a small platform. Each ndop was made for a reigning or remembered king and bears his personal emblem (ibol), a drum, a weapon, or a game board carved beside the seat, while the pattern of scarification on the torso identifies the individual monarch. The figures were kept in the sacred houses of the palace, guarded by the king's titleholders, and were brought out in ceremonies where they stood for the continuity of the throne. Despite the name, the ndop is not a naturalistic likeness but an idealised image of royal authority, and scholars disagree over whether some figures were carved after the king's death as memorials. The oldest surviving examples date to the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and a group of them was carried from the capital during the colonial expeditions before entering the British Museum and other collections. They remain the most celebrated images of Kuba kingship.
source: Kuba royal tradition; museum collections (British Museum)

name: Kalinga Royal Drum
description: The Kalinga was the most sacred drum of the Rwandan court, the principal of the four royal drums that together stood for the kingship of the mwami. Kept in a sacred house where a fire burned day and night, the drum was never allowed to touch the ground and was rubbed with bull's blood and herbs to renew its power. According to oral tradition the Kalinga reached the court with the seventeenth-century king Ruganzu II Ndori, and it travelled with the king on campaign, acquiring personal names as if it were a living ruler. The Kalinga stood for the male principle and the king, its companion drum for the queen mother, and Rwandans said 'he is king who has the drums': beating it at coronations, harvests, and victories affirmed the dynasty's authority. After the monarchy was abolished in the early 1960s the royal drums vanished from public sight, and no trace of the originals has been found, though the drums live on in the country's drumming tradition and in the re-created court dances of the Intore.
source: Rwandan court tradition; historical accounts

name: Kabyle Earthenware
description: Kabyle earthenware is the red-clay pottery of the Great Kabylia mountains of northern Algeria, a craft kept almost exclusively in the hands of women. The pots are built by hand from coils of local clay, without a wheel, then burnished with a pebble while still damp and painted before firing with geometric patterns in black, beige and red. The repertoire includes water jars, storage pots, and wide platters used to serve couscous at weddings and other feasts, and the interior of each piece is divided into circles, checkerboards, crosses and triangles that radiate from the centre. These motifs are named and read by the women who make them, and they are believed to carry meanings of supernatural protection and fertility, some of which are shared with the diamond patterns of Amazigh weaving, jewellery and facial tattoos. Because the recipes for clay, paints and firing are handed down from mother to daughter, each pot carries the imprint of a lineage, though the regional styles differ from village to village across the massif.
source: Kabyle women's pottery tradition

name: Katar
culture: Deccan and South Indian martial culture
description: The katar is the Indian punch dagger, a straight, usually double-edged blade set between two parallel side bars that form an H-shaped grip, the whole weapon being pushed forward with the fist like a punch. Because the palm push concentrates the whole force of the arm behind a single point, the katar could pierce mail and helmets in close combat, and it became the characteristic weapon of Rajput and Maratha warriors from about the 16th century onward. In addition to the plain fighting blade there were katar with wavy edges, double blades and side blades, and the wealthiest owners carried gold-damascened pieces with jewelled hilts that were as much jewellery as arms. The katar was also a ceremonial object, presented as a token of loyalty or reward and displayed in processions, and a small katar could be carried concealed in the waistband. Because it is unique to South Asia, the katar is one of the most discussed Indian weapons in the history of arms and armour.
source: Arms museum collections and temple sculpture

name: Khanda
description: The khanda is the broad, straight, double-edged sword of the Indian subcontinent, heavier and stiffer than the curved tulwar, and it is principally associated with the Sikhs of the Punjab and with the Marathas of western India. In Sikh tradition the khanda is the emblem of the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, and the central motif of the Nishan Sahib, the tall flag of a gurdwara, which shows a double-edged khanda with a chakkar (discus) and two kirpans arranged around it. The sword was carried as a weapon of war in the 17th and 18th centuries and remains a ceremonial and ritual object, used at the initiation ceremony of Amrit, where the sacred syrup is stirred with a khanda, and kept in reverence in Sikh homes and temples. Because the double edge and straight blade allowed a powerful, chopping stroke, the khanda was well suited to the tested cavalry work of the Sikh and Maratha armies. The same term is used in Sanskrit and Hindi for any large sword, so the object carries a long martial lineage beyond the Sikh faith.
source: Sikh religious tradition and panthic practice

name: Kirpan
description: The kirpan is the curved sword or dagger that an initiated Sikh wears as one of the five Ks, the panj kakkar, along with unshorn hair (kesh), a comb (kanga), a steel bangle (kara) and the cotton undergarment (kachera). Introduced at the founding of the Khalsa in 1699 by Guru Gobind Singh, the kirpan embodies the Sikh duty to defend the weak and to stand against injustice, and it is worn constantly as a reminder of that responsibility. The size and form of the kirpan vary with the community and the wearer's circumstances, from a small symbolically worn blade in parts of the diaspora to the long ceremonial kirpan of Amritdhari Sikhs, and it is treated not as an offensive weapon but as a sacred article of faith. In Sikh scripture and hagiography the kirpan is praised as the protector of the oppressed, and the five Ks together mark the body of a Sikh as the visible form of the faith. Legal accommodations for the kirpan exist in several countries, and the practice remains an active case study in religious freedom law.
source: Sikh Rahit Maryada (code of conduct)

name: Kada Bangle
description: The kada, also spelled kara, is the unadorned steel or iron bangle worn by Sikhs on the right wrist, one of the five Ks prescribed at the founding of the Khalsa in 1699. Because it is a closed circle without beginning or end, the bangle is understood as a reminder that God is eternal and without form, and its touch on the wrist constantly recalls the wearer to righteous conduct and restraint. The plain steel of the traditional kada contrasts with the gold ornaments worn by many Hindus and Muslims, signalling that a Sikh should live simply and without attachment to display. In the Punjab the broad steel kada is also worn by non-Sikhs as an item of dress, and in combat the heavy circular bangle could be used as a guard and a blunt knuckle-weapon. The kada is one of the most visible articles of Sikh identity, worn in the workplace, in court and at the gurdwara.
source: Sikh Rahit Maryada (code of conduct)

name: Kandyan Crown
description: The Kandyan crown is the royal crown of the Kandyan kingdom of Sri Lanka, the last independent Sinhalese state, which fell to the British in 1815. The crown, of gold richly set with rubies, sapphires and other gems, was worn by the kings of Kandy at great coronation ceremonies and processions, and it carried the whole sovereignty of the kingdom, so that possession of the crown was taken to mean possession of the realm. When the Kandyan chiefs signed the Kandyan Convention of 1815, the regalia, including the crown and the throne, was handed to the British and sent to England, and tradition records memorials of the crown at Windsor Castle, where the regalia long remained. In Sri Lankan memory the loss of the crown is bound up with legend: omens, the fall of a star and other portents are said to have accompanied its removal, and the crown is still popularly spoken of as the sign of a sovereignty that was not handed back. Today the Kandyan crown is remembered through replicas and regalia kept in museums, and the original remains the subject of scholarly dispute between the United Kingdom and Sri Lanka.
source: Museum holdings and Kandyan court records (British Museum collections)

name: Kastane Sword
description: The kastane is the traditional ceremonial sword of the Kandyan kingdom of Sri Lanka, worn at court as a mark of office and carried in procession, and it is one of the most characteristic creations of Sinhalese metalwork. Its signature feature is the hilt, whose pommel is carved as the head of a lion, the symbol of the Sinhalese people, often in ivory, horn or silver, with the guard and quillons finished with makara heads and scrollwork; the blade itself was frequently a European hanger or cuttoe blade imported by the Dutch and riveted into the local hilt. The kastane was not primarily a battlefield weapon but a dress sword, the attribute of chiefs, princes and royal officials, and it also entered the world of Sinhalese ritual, being used in the masked devil dances and exorcism rites in which the sanni demons and Gara Yakka are invoked. In those rituals the flashing blade is used to dominate the demons and sweep away the evil they represent, linking the courtly sword to the folk religion of the low country. Museums classify the kastane among the finest of Sri Lankan arms, and modern reproductions still accompany Kandyan dancers and drummers.
source: Museum collections and ritual ethnography (J Intangible Cultural Heritage)

name: Karahi
description: The karahi is the deep rounded pan of Pakistan, forged from cast iron or pressed steel, with two handles and steep sides, set over an open flame to cook the spiced stew that shares its name. The name of the vessel has passed to the dish itself, and a karahi of lamb, chicken or vegetables cooked with tomato, green chilli and ginger is one of the most familiar foods of Pakistani homes, roadside dhabas and bazaars, served hot straight from the pan with fresh naan. Because the karahi sits directly on the fire, the oil and spices fry hard before liquid is added, giving the gravy its characteristic rich colour and edge. It is the daily cooking vessel of many households and the centre of festive and communal meals, and iron karahis are prized for seasoning with use, so that old pans are handed down within families.
source: Pakistani domestic culinary tradition

name: Khukuri
description: The khukuri is the curved blade of the Nepali Gurkha tradition, broad and heavy near the tip, tapering to the hilt, and used for cutting wood, clearing brush, daily chores and ceremonial display. The name is spelled kukri in British usage, and the blade is forged by Nepali kamis, the metal-working caste, who shape it at a charcoal forge and temper the cutting edge while leaving the spine soft enough to absorb shock. It is carried in a leather scabbard together with two smaller knives, the karda for fine work and the chakmak for sharpening, and the distinctive notch at the blade's base is a mark of the traditional shape. A well-known folk saying holds that once the khukuri is drawn it must taste blood before being sheathed again, a custom linked to its history as a weapon of war and to the rituals of the Gurkha regiments.
source: Nepali folk custom and Gurkha regimental tradition

name: Khyber Knife
description: The khyber knife is the long, straight-backed belt knife of the frontier regions of Afghanistan and the border country of the Khyber Pass, with a wide spine, a single cutting edge and a simple handle of horn, bone or wood. It is worn at the belt and used for cutting, skinning and defence, and the name comes from the pass that links the Afghan highlands with the plains, a corridor of trade and conflict for centuries. Frontier bladesmiths forged the knives for daily work and for display, and the handles of older examples are often incised or decorated, showing the owner's pride in the weapon. The khyber knife appears in the material culture of the borderlands and in ethnographic collections of frontier weaponry, a practical tool that also served as a mark of the bearer.
material: steel, horn or bone handle, leather
source: Ethnographic collections of frontier weaponry

name: Kuchi Jewelry
description: The kuchi jewelry is the heavy silver ornament of the Kuchi, the nomadic herding people of Afghanistan, who carry their wealth on their persons in the form of large necklaces, headpieces, earrings, bracelets and belt buckles. The pieces are made of silver, often with added amber, carnelian, turquoise and glass beads, and the forms echo ancient styles of Central Asia, with coin-rimmed discs, stamped patterns and chains that jingle as the wearer moves. For a nomadic family, jewelry is a portable bank, and for a bride the dowry ornaments show the status and resources of the two families. Kuchi jewelry is made by silversmiths who work for the nomad trade, and older pieces are collected and reused, so the ornaments carry the history of generations of wandering life across the Afghan plains.
source: Ethnographic documentation of Kuchi material culture

name: Kākahu (Māori Cloak)
description: The kakahu is the woven cloak of the Maori, made from the muka fibre of the flax plant and covered with the down, feathers and tags of native birds, and worn as a cloak of rank and prestige. The weaver prepares the flax fibre, spins and dyes it, and weaves the body of the cloak on a small loom, then decorates it with feathers of kiwi, kaka, huia and other birds, or with tags of dog skin and fibre. The finest cloaks, such as the kahu kiwi, were made over months and were worn by chiefs on great occasions, and each cloak carries its own name and history. The black-feathered korowai with hanging tags is among the best-known forms, and kakahu are still woven today and worn at hui and ceremonies, treasured as taonga of the iwi that own them.
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Māori weaving and taonga

name: Kete (Māori Basket)
description: The kete is the woven basket of the Maori, plaited from the strips of the harakeke flax plant and used to carry food, tools, feathers and other goods in daily life. Plain kete are made quickly for carrying, while the patterned kete whakairo is woven with a coloured design and given as a mark of respect. In Maori tradition the three kete of knowledge were brought down from the heavens by the god Tane, who returned with the basket of ritual knowledge, the basket of ancestral knowledge and the basket of practical knowledge, and so established learning among humankind. The kete is therefore both an everyday object and a powerful image of knowledge itself, and the phrase to hand over a kete of knowledge means to teach. Kete are still woven today in the traditional materials and patterns.
source: Māori oral tradition; ethnographic records of weaving

name: Kundu Drum
description: Hourglass hand drum of Papua New Guinea, carved from a single block of light hardwood with a membrane of lizard or snake skin stretched over the open head and held with wax and resin studs, which also tune the drum. It is played with the palm and fingers, its patterns of beats belonging to the village and its ancestors; in the Sepik region the Iatmul associate the drum with the crocodile-creator, and the instrument is used in initiation rites, spirit cults, mourning and the sing-sing gatherings that draw communities together. The kundu is so emblematic that it appears on the national coat of arms, and a fine carved example is a valued heirloom handed down through families.
material: wood, lizard or snake skin, resin
source: Ethnomusicological studies of Melanesian music

name: Kryždirbystė Cross
description: Carved oak wayside crosses of the Lithuanian cross-crafting tradition, one to five metres tall, with small roofs, carved figures and flower and geometric ornament, standing at village entrances, crossroads, cemeteries and shrines. Once consecrated by a priest, a cross is sacred and draws offerings — food, rosaries, scarves and aprons — seeking fertility, healing or protection, and the craft's masters, the kryždirbiai, shape stogastulpiai, koplytstulpiai and full crosses in styles that vary from region to region. Under Russian imperial rule and again under the Soviet occupation the wayside cross became a symbol of national identity, and in 2001 the tradition was proclaimed by UNESCO a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Cross-crafting and its symbolism (2001); LNKC Savadas (Lithuanian National Culture Centre)

name: Kanklės
description: Archaic Lithuanian plucked box zither, a trapezoid of solid wood — maple, linden or ash — hollowed from a single piece and strung with parallel strings, of the same Baltic psaltery family as the Latvian kokle and the Estonian kannel. Old belief held that the bards, the vaidilos, sang heroic songs and served the gods to its music, and that the best instrument wood was cut between a person's death and funeral, for a mourned tree lent the kanklės a sorrowful, spirit-voiced tone. The instrument accompanied wedding songs and dances, its players, the kanklininkai, being honoured guests, and it was revived in the twentieth-century folk revival as a national instrument.
material: maple, linden or ash wood, wire or gut strings
source: LNKC survey of Lithuanian string instruments (chordophones); Lithuanian ethnomusicology

name: Kokle
description: The Latvian plucked box zither: a trapezoid soundbox with parallel strings over a flat board, carved from maple, ash or lime, played by strumming and plucking. A chronicle entry of 1225, when Henricus de Lettis wrote of a kokle played by Livonian youths, makes it the oldest documented psaltery in Europe, and Latvian folk songs call its strings 'silver war' and 'golden war'. The kokle accompanied the dainas, the great corpus of Latvian folksong, and in the twentieth century a larger concert kokle was developed; in 2008 the kokle and the art of koklēšana were placed in the Latvian Cultural Canon as the national instrument.
material: maple or ash wood, metal strings
source: Latvijas Kultūras kanons: Kokles un koklēšana (2008); Henricus de Lettis (1225)

name: Kihnu Woolen Skirt
description: The striped woolen skirt and knitted garments of Kihnu Island's women: bright red, green and blue striped cloth woven on home looms from local wool, worn with embroidered blouses, sashes, mittens and stockings whose colours and patterns recall old legends. With the island's men long at sea, Kihnu's women carried the culture of the island, and the making of these garments — together with the songs, dances and handicraft skills of the Kihnu cultural space inscribed by UNESCO in 2003 — became an emblem of Estonian island identity. The striped skirt, folded and held by a woven belt, is still worn daily by older women and with pride at festivals.
source: UNESCO: Kihnu cultural space (2003); Kihnu women's handicraft tradition

name: Kirivöö Belt
description: The kirivöö, the Estonian pick-up patterned belt: a narrow woven band of wool over a linen or wool ground, carrying rows of small crosses, rhombuses, triangles and diagonal figures worked by the pick-up technique. Each parish knew its own edge patterns, so that the belt could tell where a woman came from, and the belts were worn wrapped at the waist with folk dress, and given as gifts, love-pledges and protective charms. The Estonian National Museum holds belts from across the country, and studies of the small patterns at the belt edges continue to map the regional styles and their meanings.
source: Studia Vernacula: 'Small patterns at the edges of belts' (Estonian National Museum, 2018)

name: Kraków Szopka
description: The Kraków szopka is a Nativity crib built as a glittering model of the city itself, cramming Wawel Cathedral, St Mary's Basilica, castle towers, spires and arcades into a many-storeyed facade of cardboard, tin foil and painted paper around the central stable. The tradition took shape in the nineteenth century, when Kraków bricklayers and building workers made portable cribs to earn money at Christmas, and it gained its civic form after 1937, when the first official contest was held; makers known as krakowianie still compete every first Thursday of December on the Main Market Square beside the Adam Mickiewicz monument. The best szopki show great technical ambition, with moving figures, hidden candle-lit interiors and window scenes re-enacting nativity and patriotic tableaux. In 2018 UNESCO inscribed the szopka tradition on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and collections such as the one in the Historical Museum of the City of Kraków preserve competition winners going back decades.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Kraków ethnography

name: Kukeri
description: The kukeri are the masked dancers of the Bulgarian winter, men dressed from head to foot in sheepskin and goat-hide, crowned with tall carved wooden masks and hung about the waist with heavy bronze and copper bells, who process through villages around New Year and before Lent. Their dance - a hopping, swaying, bell-shaking performance - is meant to drive out evil spirits, ill luck and sickness and to bring health, fertility and a good harvest in the season to come. Masks differ from region to region: Pernik favours towering feathered and horned figures, while the Rhodope makers carve flatter, beast-like faces, and each costume can weigh tens of kilograms. Since 1966 the International Festival of Masquerade Games Surva in Pernik has gathered hundreds of groups every January, and in 2015 UNESCO inscribed the Surova folk feast of the Pernik region on the Representative List.
material: sheepskin, carved wood, goat hair, bronze bells
source: Bulgarian ethnography of winter ritual customs

name: Kantsi (Georgian Drinking Horn)
description: The kantsi is the drinking horn of the Georgian highlands, cut from the curved horn of an ox, aurochs or mountain goat, polished, and often mounted at the rim in chased silver, sometimes with a small stand or a chain to hang it by. It is the fixed vessel of the supra, the Georgian feast, where the tamada raises the horn for each toast and custom requires it to be drained to the bottom in one draught before it is passed on; to drink from the kantsi is to honour the wine, the host and the speaker. The largest horns, holding a litre or more, are prized heirlooms of Svaneti and Khevsureti, and the same vessels appear in medieval Georgian manuscripts and in modern feast painting. Because the horn cannot be set down with wine in it, every toast must be finished, which is why the kantsi is remembered as the instrument of Georgian generosity.
material: ox or goat horn, chased silver (festive examples)
source: Russian Museum of Ethnography collections; Georgian feast (supra) custom studies

name: Khachkar (Armenian Cross-Stone)
description: The khachkar is the Armenian cross-stone, a freestanding stele carved from a single slab of local stone, most often the volcanic tuff of the Armenian plateau, its face dominated by an ornamented cross set over a rosette or a wheel of eternity. Around the cross the carver fills the stone with interlace, vine scrolls, leaves, pomegranates and birds, and the whole composition is framed in a decorated border; the earliest dated example bears the year 879, and the art reached its richest period from the thirteenth century. Khachkars were raised as tombstones, memorials for the dead, church dedications and thanksgivings, linking the everyday and the divine, the village and the monastery. In 2010 UNESCO inscribed the symbolism and craftsmanship of khachkars on the Representative List, and carved examples stand at Armenian churches from Julfa to Jerusalem.
material: volcanic tuff or other local stone
source: UNESCO ICH 'Armenian cross-stones art. Symbolism and craftsmanship of Khachkars' (2010)

name: Kamancha (Azerbaijani Spike Fiddle)
description: The kamancha is the bowed spike fiddle of Azerbaijan, built with a spherical or bowl-shaped wooden body covered with fish- or lambskin, a long neck that pierces the body, and four steel strings, played upright with the bow resting on the knee. Its bright, precise tone carries well indoors, which is why the kamancha sits beside the tar in the mugham trio and in the ensembles of Azerbaijani folk music, doubling and answering the melodic line. The instrument has a long history across the Caucasus, Persia and Central Asia under the name kamancheh, and Azerbaijani craftsmen and players developed their own distinguished school. In 2017 UNESCO inscribed the art of crafting and playing the kamancha on the Representative List, and the instrument remains central both to classical mugham and to the folk music of weddings and festivals.
material: walnut or mulberry wood, skin soundboard, steel strings
source: UNESCO ICH 'Art of crafting and playing with kamancha' (2017)

name: Kelaghayi (Azerbaijani Silk Headscarf)
description: The kelaghayi is the square silk headscarf of Azerbaijani women, woven on narrow silk looms in the town of Sheki and the village of Basgal, then dyed and printed with woodblocks so that a patterned border frames a plainer field. The classic ornament is the buta, the curved teardrop or flame motif that runs along the edge, and the colours carry meaning: white and light shades for older women and mourning, red and bright colours for brides and young women. The scarf is folded and tied in many ways - under the chin, at the back, or draped over the shoulders - and it belongs to daily wear, weddings, funerals and religious observance alike, its symbolism bound up with the woman's age and occasion. In 2014 UNESCO inscribed the traditional art and symbolism of the kelaghayi on the Representative List, and silk masters in Basgal still print the scarves by hand.
era: silk tradition from c. 7th century; kelaghayi to present
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art and symbolism of Kelaghayi' (2014)

name: Koschei's Needle
description: Needle in which the Russian fairy-tale villain Koschei the Deathless hides his soul, so that he cannot be killed while it remains intact. In Afanasyev's collected tales the needle lies inside an egg, the egg inside a duck, the duck inside a hare, and the hare inside a chest locked on an island oak; the hero must open each container in turn and break the needle to destroy Koschei. The motif recurs across Slavic and wider folklore, and variants replace the needle with a flower, a spider or a bird's egg. Folklorists class it among the 'external soul' tales, in which a being stores its life force outside its body for safety; the moment the chain of containers is broken, the villain collapses and dies. The needle is therefore the hinge of the whole story, and the hero's task becomes one of patience and sequence rather than of strength.
material: iron needle (in the tale, nested in egg, duck, hare, chest)
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' (Koschei the Deathless)

name: Kokoshnik (Russian Women's Headdress)
description: Crest-shaped ceremonial headdress of Russian women, a stiff crown of brocade, velvet or silk embroidered with pearls, gold thread and beads. Worn over the braids from the 17th century, the kokoshnik varied by region, from horned and high-crested to flat-topped forms, and marked the married woman; after Peter the Great's court reforms it survived as festive wear in the provinces. The word derives from 'kokosh', the old Russian name for a hen or cockerel, from the crest-like shape, and the headdress was worn at weddings and church festivals together with the best dress. Regional types carry distinct names, such as the one-horned kika of Tula and the morshen of the north, each built on a stiffened cardboard or birch-bark base covered in rich fabric. Museums hold examples sewn with river pearls, and the form has been revived on the stage, in film and in neo-Russian fashion, making it one of the most recognisable images of Russian national costume.
material: brocade, velvet, silk, pearls, gold thread
source: Russian Ethnographic Museum; historic Russian dress studies

name: Kamcha (Kazakh Whip)
description: Braided leather whip of the Kazakhs, carried by horsemen and elders as a riding tool and badge of authority. In Kazakh folklore the kamcha carried protective power: the whip of a respected man was hung near a woman in childbirth, and its crack was said to drive off evil spirits. Skilled craftsmen braid the lash from several plaited leather cords. The handle is carved of wood or bone, often ornamented with silver, and the lash tapers from the handle to a thin tip that cracks sharply in the air when snapped. In the steppe the kamcha was as much a tool of the herd as of the saddle, used to guide horses and cattle at a distance, and an elder carried it as a mark of rank and command. Kazakh custom holds that the whip is never pointed at a person, and a man leaving on a journey might hang his kamcha over the threshold as protection for the house.
material: braided leather, wood or bone handle
source: e-history.kz 'The role of the horse in Kazakh culture' (2016); Kazinform feature on whip-braiding

name: Kalfak (Tatar Women's Embroidered Cap)
description: Velvet cap worn by Tatar women, richly embroidered with gold thread, pearls and gilt coins, with a long embroidered tail or tassel hanging down the back. Part of a woman's dowry, the kalfak was the most original piece of Tatar women's festive headwear and demanded great skill in gold embroidery; unlike the man's tubeteika it marked marital status and rank. The cap is sewn in a crescent or beaked shape that sits toward the back of the head, its velvet embroidered in gold thread laid in tight couched stitches, with a pendant band falling to the shoulder. In the 19th century married and unmarried women wore different forms, and the kalfak was trimmed with pearls, sequins and small gilt coins that rattled softly as the wearer moved. Embroidering a kalfak could take weeks of exacting work, and girls prepared them as gifts within the trousseau. Kazan museums display 19th-century examples, and the kalfak is now revived in festive dress and on the stage.
material: velvet, gold thread, pearls, gilt coins
source: tatarstan.ru 'Clothes and trappings'; National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan

name: Kumgan (Tatar Copper Ewer)
description: Narrow-necked copper or brass ewer with a spout and handle used by the Tatars for water and for the ritual ablution before Muslim prayer. Made by Tatar coppersmiths (bakyrche), the kumgan was a symbol of the Tatar home, kept with a towelled basin and used at festivals and religious observances. Kazan and the villages of Zakazanye produced the finest examples. The ewer's long spout and slender neck pour a controlled stream, and the body is often engraved with floral or geometric ornament; some examples carry a lid and a pierced foot. The kumgan is used in the washing that precedes prayer, and its shape reflects centuries of contact between Volga Tatar craftsmen and the metalwork of Central Asia and the Middle East. In the 18th and 19th centuries the coppersmiths of Kazan and its surrounding villages supplied ewers, basins and kettles far beyond the Volga, and their work was praised at the great fairs. Museum collections preserve kumgans from the 16th to the 19th century, showing the craft's long and steady development.
maker: Tatar coppersmiths (bakyrche), Kazan and Zakazanye workshops
source: ar.culture.ru 'Kumgan' (Tatarstan museums); National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan

name: Khomus (Yakut Jew's Harp)
description: Metal Jew's harp of the Yakut (Sakha) people, an elongated iron frame with a flexible steel tongue, played by plucking the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The khomus imitates bird calls and natural sounds, accompanied songs and held shamanic associations. Yakutsk's Khomus Museum, the republic's Khomus Day and an international festival honour it as a symbol of Sakha culture. The player holds the frame against the teeth and strikes the tongue with a finger, shaping the note with the mouth and breath, so that a single harp produces a shifting range of overtones. The khomus is among the oldest of instruments, with wooden and bone examples and a metal specimen dated around the 3rd to 1st centuries BC attributed to the Xiongnu. The Yakut khomus is sometimes said to have been made first from the wood or bone of a tree struck by lightning, and later from iron, in the shape of the horseshoe that frames the tongue. Its repertoire includes pieces for healing, for the dance, and for imitating the sounds of the taiga.
material: iron or steel frame and tongue
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Khomus'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections; Khomus Museum, Yakutsk
